The confidence interval widths expand substantially as the horizon lengthens, which is a direct reflection of how uncertainty compounds over time in commodity markets. At the 1-day horizon, the interval is relatively tight at roughly plus or minus $2.20, consistent with typical daily volatility in crude oil of around 1–2%. By one week, the interval widens to nearly $5 on each side, and by one month it stretches to roughly $10 in either direction. Specific risks that could push prices outside the stated intervals on the downside include a sharper-than-expected slowdown in Chinese demand, a surprise increase in OPEC+ production quotas, or a broad risk-off episode in financial markets that strengthens the dollar and weighs on commodities. A meaningful deterioration in global manufacturing activity could also undercut demand assumptions. It is also worth acknowledging that oil markets can experience sudden gap moves — triggered by weekend geopolitical events, surprise OPEC announcements, or major macroeconomic data releases — that the smooth confidence intervals I provided do not fully capture. The intervals assume a relatively continuous price process, but the real distribution of oil price outcomes has fat tails, meaning extreme moves are more likely than a normal distribution would suggest. Anyone relying on these forecasts should treat the outer bounds as genuinely possible but not exhaustive of the full range of outcomes.
